title: Effective Governance for Boards and Directors
summary: A twelve-module programme covering the standards expected of individual directors and the practices that make a board effective, for regulated firms, fund boards and management companies.
intro: This training programme equips boards and directors with the duties, standards and practical skills of effective governance: who should sit on the board, what each director is accountable for, and how a board works well in practice.

sections.Aim and Purpose: To give directors of regulated firms, fund boards and management companies a complete grounding in effective governance, from the standards expected of each director to the dynamics that decide whether a board actually oversees the business. Participants leave able to evidence their fitness, independence and reasonable steps, and to improve how their board is chaired, informed and evaluated.
sections.What It Covers: Good governance, directors' duties, fitness and probity, independence and time commitment, board composition and diversity, delegation and oversight, conflicts of interest, individual accountability, the chair and the agenda, board information, boardroom dynamics, and board evaluation.
Intended Audience: Chairs, executive, non-executive and independent directors of regulated firms, fund boards and management companies
Senior managers preparing for a first board appointment or moving from an executive to a non-executive role
Company secretaries, heads of governance and compliance staff who support the board and its committees
Learning Objectives: Explain what good governance requires of a regulated board and how it differs from general corporate governance
Apply directors' duties and fitness and probity standards to their own role and appointments
Assess board composition, independence, tenure and diversity against good practice
Oversee delegated functions and conflicts of interest so that responsibility is demonstrably retained
Evidence reasonable steps under an individual accountability regime
Improve the board's agenda, information, challenge and decision-making, and design a board effectiveness action plan
sections.Structure and Format: Twelve modules of about two hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, typically as a three- to four-day programme or as a series of board briefing sessions. Part one covers the individual director; part two covers how the board works as a team. Modules can be selected or tailored for a fund, management company or other regulated firm.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Board or senior management experience in financial services is helpful. No prior governance training is required.
Core Reading: IOSCO, Examination of Governance for Collective Investment Schemes (2006–2007)
FSB, Strengthening Governance Frameworks to Mitigate Misconduct Risk: A Toolkit for Firms and Supervisors (2018)
Olivier Sibony, You're About to Make a Terrible Mistake! How Biases Distort Decision-Making (2020)

modules.title: What Good Governance Looks Like
modules.summary: What governance is for in a regulated firm or fund, what good, bad and failed governance look like in practice, and why governing a fund or licensee differs from governing an ordinary company.
objectives: Define governance in terms of the interests the board must serve
Distinguish good, poor and failed governance using real enforcement outcomes
Map the parties around the board: owners, regulators, managers and delegates
syllabus: Purpose of governance: acting efficiently and exclusively in investors' and customers' interests
Good governance: clear responsibilities, documented policies and structures that foster challenge
When governance fails: lessons from regulatory fines and misconduct cases
The distinctive features of fund and regulated-firm governance

modules.title: The Role of the Director: Duties and Collective Responsibility
modules.summary: The legal duties a director owes, the different roles of executive, non-executive and independent directors and the chair, and how individual responsibility sits alongside the board's collective decision-making.
objectives: Explain the core duties of a director and to whom they are owed
Compare the roles of executive, non-executive and independent directors
Balance individual responsibility with the board's collective accountability
syllabus: Statutory and fiduciary duties: skill, care, diligence and acting in good faith
Is there a job description for a director of a fund or a management company?
Executive, non-executive, independent and chair roles on the board and its committees
Individual versus collective responsibility and protecting against liability

modules.title: Fitness and Probity
modules.summary: The standards of competence, honesty, integrity and financial soundness that directors must meet, how regulators act as gatekeepers at appointment, and how firms assess fitness on an ongoing basis.
objectives: Apply fitness and probity standards to directors and other key roles
Prepare for a regulatory fitness and probity assessment or interview
Recognise the circumstances that call fitness or probity into question
syllabus: Competent and capable: qualifications, experience, competence and capacity
Honest, ethical and acting with integrity, including non-financial misconduct
Financial soundness and the firm's due diligence and certification
Regulatory gatekeeping, interviews, refusals and lessons from case law

modules.title: Independence of Mind and Time Commitment
modules.summary: What it means to bring independence of mind to the board, the threats to independence in practice, and how directors and boards judge whether a director has enough time for the role.
objectives: Distinguish formal independence from independence of mind
Identify relationships and incentives that threaten independent judgement
Assess time commitment and the risks of multiple directorships
syllabus: Independence of mind: sound, objective and independent decisions
Threats to independence: tenure, fees, group links and personal relationships
Time commitment: what is sufficient and how boards evidence it
Multiple directorships, capacity limits and regulatory scrutiny

modules.title: Board Composition: Appointment, Tenure, Succession and Diversity
modules.summary: How to build a board with the right mix of skills, independence and perspectives, the due diligence a director should complete before accepting an appointment, and how to manage tenure, refreshment and succession.
objectives: Design a board composition and skills matrix for a regulated firm or fund
Carry out due diligence before accepting a board appointment
Plan tenure, refreshment, succession and diversity objectives
syllabus: Board size, balance of non-executive and independent directors, and skills matrices
Due diligence before accepting an offer: good practice and red flags
Tenure limits, board refreshment and succession planning
Diversity of skills, background and thinking, barriers and effective initiatives

modules.title: Delegation and Oversight: Retaining Responsibility
modules.summary: Delegation is permitted but responsibility is retained. This module covers how the board decides what to delegate, how it oversees delegates and service providers, and what effective oversight looks like to a regulator.
objectives: Explain which decisions the board must retain and which it may delegate
Design an oversight framework for delegates and service providers
Evidence effective oversight through reporting, dialogue and escalation
syllabus: Delegation permitted, responsibility retained: reserved matters and delegated authority
The relationship between the board, the management company and delegates
Reporting, open dialogue and the board's right to information from delegates
Regulatory findings on delegate oversight and the reasonable steps expected

modules.title: Conflicts of Interest
modules.summary: How conflicts arise for boards and individual directors, including in group structures, smaller firms and multiple directorships, and how they should be identified, managed, monitored and disclosed.
objectives: Identify conflicts of interest at board, group and individual level
Apply a conflicts policy, register and management arrangements
Judge when a conflict should be disclosed, mitigated or avoided altogether
syllabus: Sources of conflict: group links, delegates, fees and personal interests
Multiple directorships and full-time roles elsewhere in the group
Smaller firms and condensed structures: when senior staff wear several hats
Conflicts registers, board minutes and evidencing that conflicts are managed

modules.title: Individual Accountability and Reasonable Steps
modules.summary: Individual accountability regimes and what they mean for directors: prescribed responsibilities, responsibilities maps, conduct standards and the duty to take reasonable steps, illustrated through enforcement cases against senior individuals.
objectives: Explain how individual accountability regimes allocate responsibility to directors
Demonstrate reasonable steps for the areas a director is responsible for
Draw lessons from enforcement action against chairs and directors
syllabus: Senior executive accountability regimes around the world and their common features
Inherent and prescribed responsibilities, responsibilities maps and statements
Conduct standards and the duty of responsibility: what reasonable steps look like
Enforcement case studies, personal liability and directors' and officers' insurance

modules.title: The Chair, the Agenda and the Company Secretary
modules.summary: The pivotal role of the chair in setting the tone and running effective meetings, how to manage agenda overload and time, and the role of the company secretary and pre-board engagement.
objectives: Describe the responsibilities and attributes of an effective chair
Design an agenda that prioritises strategy, risk and key decisions
Use the company secretary and pre-board engagement to strengthen meetings
syllabus: The chair's responsibilities, attributes and relationship with the chief executive
Agenda overload: frequency, duration, committees and priorities
Agenda rules: important topics first, timed items and clear decisions
The company secretary, pre-board meetings and minutes that evidence challenge

modules.title: Board Information: Papers, Presentations and Asymmetry
modules.summary: What good board information looks like, why oversized packs harm decisions, how to get the information the board needs without micromanaging, and how directors handle technical topics such as technology and AI.
objectives: Evaluate board papers against the qualities of good information
Reduce information asymmetry between management and non-executives
Engage with technical presentations and know what questions to ask
syllabus: Good information: accurate, timely, clear, comparable and focused on decisions
Board pack size, information overload and cover papers that state the question
Information asymmetry, independent assurance and the fear of micromanaging
Technical topics, technology and AI: building enough knowledge to challenge

modules.title: Boardroom Dynamics: Challenge, Culture and Decision-Making
modules.summary: How boardroom culture, personalities and bias shape decisions, how to challenge well, and practical counter-measures against group think, dominant voices and poor decision-making.
objectives: Recognise the risk factors for poor board decision-making
Challenge constructively and handle difficult board members
Apply counter-measures to group think and judgemental bias
syllabus: Risk factors for poor decisions: dominant voices, time pressure and isolation
Challenge well: preparation, curiosity and a bracing rather than collegial culture
Difficult personalities, non-attendance and managing difficult conversations
Heuristics, framing and group think, and practical counter-measures

modules.title: Keeping the Board Effective: Evaluation, Development and Action Plan
modules.summary: How boards evaluate themselves, what regulators look for in board effectiveness reviews, how directors keep their skills current, and a capstone in which each participant builds a board effectiveness action plan.
objectives: Design an internal or externally facilitated board evaluation
Plan ongoing development for the board and individual directors
Produce a practical board effectiveness action plan
syllabus: Board evaluation: scope, methods, frequency and acting on findings
What supervisors look for in board effectiveness reviews
Director development, upskilling and moving from executive to non-executive
Capstone: a board effectiveness action plan for each participant

related.title: Board Effectiveness: Dynamics and Decision-Making
related.summary: A ten-module programme helping boards strengthen their dynamics, information and decision-making, and evidence effective oversight to supervisors.

related.title: Culture, Conduct and Accountability for Boards
related.summary: An eight-module programme giving boards the tools to shape and oversee culture, align incentives, hold individuals to account and evidence oversight to regulators.

related.title: Finance and Prudential Essentials for Directors of Regulated Firms
related.summary: An eight-module programme giving non-financial directors the confidence to read a regulated firm's accounts, capital and liquidity position, and to challenge the CFO.

related.title: Geopolitical and Emerging Risks for Boards
related.summary: An eight-module programme helping boards identify, debate and prepare for geopolitical and emerging risks, ending with a facilitated board scenario exercise.

related.title: Group Governance and Cross-Border Operations
related.summary: A nine-module programme helping boards and senior managers of cross-border groups balance group direction with local accountability, oversee intragroup arrangements and deal with multiple supervisors.

related.title: Induction for Directors of Regulated Firms
related.summary: A ten-module induction giving new directors of regulated firms the grounding to discharge their duties, understand supervisory expectations and oversee the firm's risks.
